simplification: The State Government must give the District Commission the officers and staff it needs to help it do its work.
The state government has to give the District Commission enough workers to help it.
The chosen mediator must carry out the mediation within the time and in the way set out in the regulations.
The person picked to help both sides agree has to follow the rules about how and when to do it.

Even though sub-section (1) sets a time limit, a complaint can still be accepted after that period if the complainant shows the District, State or National Commission that there was a good reason for the delay. But the Commission must write down its reasons for excusing the delay before accepting such a complaint.
If you file a consumer complaint late, it can still be accepted if you had a good reason. The commission has to write down why it is allowing it.

Unless this Act or another law in force clearly says otherwise, an appeal can be made to the National Commission against any order that a State Commission passed in an appeal, if the National Commission is satisfied that the case raises a substantial question of law.
If a State Commission decides an appeal, you can go to the National Commission next. It will only take the case if there is an important legal question.

The National Commission can use its jurisdiction, powers and authority through its Benches. The President can form a Bench with one or more members as he thinks fit, and the most senior member of the Bench will lead it.
The National Commission can split into smaller groups to hear cases. The most senior member leads each group.
The Central Government will set up the Central Consumer Protection Council, called the Central Council, by a notification, starting from the date given in that notification.
The central government will create a group called the Central Council to look after consumers.

In addition to sub-section (1), a notice required under this Act may be sent to an electronic service provider at the address it gives on the online platform where it offers its services. For this, the electronic service provider must appoint a nodal officer to receive and handle such notices.
Online companies can be sent legal notices at the address they show on their website or app. They must name an officer to deal with these notices.

If the National Commission is satisfied that a case involves a substantial question of law, it must state that question and hear the appeal on it. However, this does not stop the National Commission from hearing the appeal on another substantial question of law, if it finds that the case involves one and writes down its reasons.
The National Commission writes down the main legal question in a case and hears the appeal on it. It can also look at other important legal questions if it explains why.
The State Government must set up, by notification, a consumer mediation cell attached to each District Commission and State Commission in the State.
Each state must create a special team at every consumer commission to help both sides settle their problems.

Every order made by a District Commission, State Commission or the National Commission will be enforced by that Commission as if it were a court decree in a civil suit. The provisions of Order XXI of the First Schedule to the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 will apply as far as possible, with every mention of a decree read as a mention of an order under this Act.
When a consumer commission makes a decision, it must be followed just like a court's decision.

The regulations will set out the qualifications and experience needed to be on the panel of mediators, how mediators are chosen and trained, their fees, the terms of being on the panel, their code of conduct, the reasons and process for removing them or cancelling their place on the panel, and other related matters.
Special rules decide who can become a mediator, how they are trained and paid, and how they can be removed.

The Central Authority will be made up of a Chief Commissioner and a prescribed number of other Commissioners, all appointed by the Central Government to use the powers and carry out the duties under this Act.
The Central Authority is run by a Chief Commissioner and some other Commissioners chosen by the central government.

Subject to the other provisions of this Act, the District Commission can hear complaints where the value of the goods or services paid for is not more than one crore rupees. However, the Central Government may set a different value if it thinks it is necessary.
The District Commission handles complaints about things or services that cost up to one crore rupees. The central government can change this amount.
A competent court will not take up any offence under sections 88 and 89 unless a complaint is filed by the Central Authority or by an officer it has authorised for this purpose.
A court will only look at these offences if the Central Authority or its officer files the complaint.

The State Commission will usually work from the State capital. It can also work at other places that the State Government, after consulting the State Commission, announces in the Official Gazette. The State Government may also set up regional benches of the State Commission at places it thinks suitable.
The State Commission usually works in the state capital, but it can also work in other places the government chooses.

If the District, State or National Commission is satisfied, based on information from the mediator or from anyone else including the parties to the complaint, and after hearing the mediator, it will replace that mediator with another one.
If there is a problem with a mediator, the consumer commission will listen to them and then replace them with someone else.
A product manufacturer is liable in a product liability case even if it proves that it was not careless or dishonest when it gave the express warranty for the product.
A company that makes a product still has to pay for harm caused, even if it didn't mean to make a false promise.

The Central Government will set up, by notification and from a date it chooses, a Central Consumer Protection Authority, called the Central Authority. Its job is to deal with violations of consumer rights, unfair trade practices, and false or misleading advertisements that harm the public and consumers, and to promote, protect and enforce the rights of consumers as a group.
The central government will create the Central Authority to protect shoppers. It stops unfair business tricks and fake or misleading ads.
A complainant can bring a product liability case against a product manufacturer, a product service provider or a product seller for any harm caused to them by a defective product.
If a broken or faulty product hurts you, you can take action against the company that made it, sold it or serviced it.

No action or proceeding of the Central Authority will become invalid just because of: (a) a vacancy in, or a defect in how the Central Authority was formed; (b) a defect in the appointment of a person acting as Chief Commissioner or Commissioner; or (c) any irregularity in its procedure that does not affect the merits of the case.
The Central Authority's decisions still count even if a seat is empty or there was a small mistake in how someone was appointed.
Once an offence has been settled under sub-section (1), no new or further case will be taken against the offender for that offence.
After an offence is settled by paying money, the person can't be taken to court again for it.
After admitting a complaint, or when a case sent for mediation has not been settled, the District Commission will go ahead with the complaint.
Once the District Commission accepts a complaint, or if talks to settle it fail, it starts working on the case.

If the parties agree to settle by mediation and give their consent in writing, the District Commission must send the matter for mediation within five days of getting that consent. In that case, the rules on mediation in Chapter V will apply.
If both sides agree in writing to talk it out, the District Commission sends the case to mediation within 5 days.

For mediation, the National, State or District Commission will prepare a panel of mediators, kept by the consumer mediation cell attached to it. The panel is made on the advice of a selection committee made up of the President and a member of that Commission.
Each consumer commission keeps a list of people who can help both sides agree. A small committee picks these people.
The purpose of every State Council is to give advice on promoting and protecting consumer rights under this Act within the State.
Each State Council gives advice on how to protect shoppers' rights in that state.

The Central Government may make rules, by notification, about the qualifications, recruitment, appointment process, term of office, resignation and removal of the President and members of the District Commission.
The central government makes the rules about who can lead the District Commission and how they are chosen or removed.
Anyone who does not follow a direction of the Central Authority under sections 20 and 21 can be punished with up to six months in prison, a fine of up to twenty lakh rupees, or both.
If you ignore an order from the Central Authority, you can go to jail or pay a big fine.

Even though the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 says otherwise, the District, State or National Commission will have the powers of a Judicial Magistrate of first class to try offences under sub-section (1). Once it has these powers, the Commission will be treated as a Judicial Magistrate of first class under that Code.
Consumer commissions can act like criminal judges when someone breaks their orders.
If the District Commission does not decide whether to admit the complaint within the set time, the complaint will be treated as admitted.
If the District Commission doesn't decide in time, your complaint is accepted automatically.
Unless stated otherwise, the District, State or National Commission will try the offences under sub-section (1) in a summary (quick) way.
These offences are handled in a fast, simple trial by the consumer commission.

The District Commission will hear every complaint based on affidavits and documents on record. However, if someone applies to be heard or to have the parties examined in person or by video conference, the District Commission may allow it if there is a good reason and it writes down its reasons.
The District Commission mostly decides cases by reading written statements and papers. Sometimes it can let people speak in person or on video.
If only part of the consumer dispute is settled, the District, State or National Commission will record the settlement of those issues and continue hearing the remaining issues in the dispute.
If only some problems are solved, the commission writes those down and keeps working on the rest.

The State Council will be an advisory council with these members: (a) the State Minister in charge of Consumer Affairs, who will be the Chairperson; (b) a prescribed number of other official or non-official members representing certain interests; and (c) up to ten other official or non-official members nominated by the Central Government.
The State Council gives advice and is led by the state's consumer affairs minister. It also has other members, including up to ten picked by the central government.
